brief: TS Lombard stays constructive on AI stocks near term: hyperscaler capex plans are unchanged, GPU rental prices show compute demand still solid, the Fed's tightening cycle has only just begun, and corrections historically see a rebound before any ultimate crash. But it tests that optimism against the first year of the Dotcom crash. The Nasdaq peaked 10 March 2000 and fell over a third by mid-April after Fed hikes (Feb 25bp, March 25bp, May 50bp), while Barron's warned Dotcoms were running out of cash. A rebound through summer, up 35% off the lows by mid-June, was driven by buy-the-dip behavior, a narrative that tech was immune to rate hikes, rotation into real-earnings names like Cisco, Oracle, Sun, Intel and Microsoft, and dollar strength. Even Fed staff endorsed the rate-immunity view near the Nasdaq's summer peak. By September housing and autos showed slowdown, Q3 earnings estimates came under pressure, credit tightened, and the Nasdaq fell over 40% in three months, finishing 2000 near half its peak. The S&P 500 held its highs for six months before following lower. TS Lombard calls this history eerily similar to today's bull case, a case for humility rather than a crash call.
